content.title: Artemis II: A beacon of light amid tensions in space - Royal Aeronautical Society
content.text: For the first time, the Artemis II crew returning to the Moon next year visited the site where the European Service Module is being developed in Bremen, Germany. BELLA RICHARDS explores why this visit was so significant, and how the Artemis programme has been a symbol of global collaboration amid the ongoing tensions on Earth, and in space.The Apollo era will forever be a significant part of space and science history, but the modern-day quest to the Moon, the Artemis programme, symbolises a new paradigm of the space industry – one of global collaboration. What was once an American-only programme has become a global one, and remains a beacon of light amid continuous international tensions, including the one’s in space. In the week that Germany became the 29th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, the Artemis II crew travelled to Bremen to meet the engineers and team behind the European Service Module (ESM), which will propel the Orion spacecraft towards the Moon next year, and to celebrate the international team working together. “As we look at national cooperation, it is not lost on us that just yesterday Germany became the 29th country to sign the Artemis Accords, which we're very proud to have Germany on board as we try to put together a truly global team for deep space exploration, [and] for the safe, sustainable use, not just with the Moon but the entire Solar System,” said Reid Wiseman, commander of the Artemis II crew at a press conference in Bremen on 15 September. Wiseman emphasised the relief of having a team from across the world supporting the astronauts when in deep space. “There's a little clause in the Artemis accords, which is if we get in trouble while we're out there, people will come and help rescue us regardless of what nation they're from, and we really appreciate that.” Regardless of certain tensions with Russia and China, space still has a distinct way of bringing nations together, rather than apart. Artemis I and II Artemis II's planned trajectory to the moon. (NASA)The Artemis programme is the modern-day return to the Moon, on behalf of NASA and its global partners, the European Space Agency (ESA), the German Aerospace Center (DLR), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), the Israel Space Agency (ISA), and the Italian Space Agency (ASI). It will be the first human return to the Moon since the Apollo 17 mission in 1972. and will also land the first woman and person of colour on the lunar surface. The programme consists of several elements, including the Orion spacecraft capsule developed by Lockheed Martin; the ESM developed by Airbus Defence and Space that powers Orion; the Space Launch System rocket; and eventually the Human Landing System (HLS), Gateway, Artemis Base Camp, and Exploration Ground Systems. Artemis I was the first of a series of trips to the Moon and saw the Orion spacecraft atop the SLS rocket lift off from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on 16 November 2022. This mission acted as a precursor to Artemis II, and focused on demonstrating Orion’s capabilities upon launch, in space, and return to Earth. The mission lasted just under 26 days. If all goes to plan, Artemis II is set to launch in November 2024, two years after the first mission. NASA astronaut’s commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch with Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen will be the first humans to return to the Moon in over 50 years. The mission is slated to last around ten days and focus on testing Orion and SLS’ capabilities, but without actually landing on the Moon. Artemis II will pave the way for future deep-space missions, such as the lunar landing, the development of Gateway which will be a multi-purpose station orbiting the Moon, and the Artemis base camp. Learning from Apollo 13 NASA astronaut’s commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch with Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen will be the first humans to return to the Moon in over 50 years. (Bella Richards/RAeS)The Apollo 13 mission was the seventh to the Moon in 1970, and saw astronauts Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert, and Fred Haise work together to get back home safely in the face of an oxygen tank failure. The spacecraft never reached the Moon, but the astronauts and mission control team were able to return the astronauts in one piece by looping around the Moon and using its gravity and the Lunar Module’s (LM) engine to propel it towards Earth. For Artemis II, there is a big focus on having contingency plans for every scenario. “Not just Apollo 13, but in general, we learn a lot from missions we fly, and we implement the things I think will help us hopefully address those things that we encounter”, Victor Glover said. Glover said the team has considered every risk and every potential failure in order to be prepared for anything during the mission. “On the Orion spacecraft, not only will we work a lot on redundancy, but we also look at manual intervention… access for the crew to understand exactly what the spacecraft is doing and what issues are happening with the subsystem.” Further, Wiseman added that the Orion spacecraft has been built in a way that the astronauts and mission control will know all the failure modes and be prepared for any scenario. “But at the end of the day, something can go wrong that you don't expect and that's why human ingenuity starts to creep its way in and we may have to solve problems that haven't been thought of and we will work with ground teams and we will get them done,” he said. The Artemis II team will train for a total of 18 months before launch – beginning in June this year – and have already been learning about Orion’s key systems, such as its displays, vehicle controls, audio and imagery systems. The crew is currently waiting for the Orion simulator to be certified and integrated at NASA NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. The simulator will replicate real life scenarios that the astronauts will have to face in space. Finally, Jeremy Hansen said that the international team is setting an example to the rest of humanity in working together to solve problems. “In Apollo 13, it gets really bad, and it gets to the point where there's kind of an iconic scene there where the flight director stops everybody, because everybody's got a failure to report, and he says ‘okay, tell me what we got left on a spacecraft that's good’ – he flipped the problem on its head because it doesn't fit the current model that we use day to day,” he said. “I love this because it points to what we have going on in the world right now and why this international collaboration is so important. It’s really easy for us in the world to point out all the failures. But what we have to do once in a while is put the problem on its head and figure out what we have left?” Europe powers a US module for the first time In the presence of one of the Artemis astronauts that will rely on the ESM-2 for water, air, electricity, propulsion and temperature control on their two-week voyage around our Moon, ESA’s European Service Module production manager Anthony Thirkettle and NASA’s Orion programme manager Howard Hu signed the papers for the handover of the hardware. (ESA)The ESM is the first time an American spacecraft will be powered by a European-build system, and its role is to provide electricity, water, oxygen, and nitrogen to Orion. In 2013, ESA was selected by NASA to contribute to the Artemis spacecraft, and since then has been contracted to develop the EMS up to Artemis VI, with the agency having invested €2 billion into the programme thus far. ESA chose Airbus Defence and Space to build the system, and over 3,000 people are working on the ESM in Europe alone, with 60 different companies involved in the process. At the press briefing, Marc Steckling, head of space exploration at Airbus, said the company has submitted two proposals to ESA to develop the module for the Artemis VII to IX missions. Meanwhile, Marc told AEROSPACE that the ESM-3 is still on track to deliver this year, most likely in December. The Bremen visit was the first time the Artemis II astronauts got up close and personal with the ESM, which will provide them their fundamental needs in space. According to ESA, the ESM has a launch mass of 13,500 kg – making up 60% of Orion’s total mass. The cylindrical system is approximately four metres in diameter and height. A total of 33 engines powers the spacecraft – like Starship. The main engine on Artemis was the repurposed Orbital Manoeuvring System that was used on previous Shuttle missions, providing 25.7 kN to the spacecraft. Eight additional R-4D-11 auxiliary thrusters built by Aerojet that each provide 490 N are onboard as a backup and to enable orbital corrections. Lastly, 24 smaller Reaction Control System engines built by ArianeGroup grouped into six pods provide altitude control to the spacecraft. Once launched and the rocket fairing is jettisoned, the ESM will deploy its solar array, unfolding to a span 19m. The system is derived from the legacy platform, ESA’s Automated Transfer Vehicle (ATV), which was used as a cargo resupply spacecraft – like Russia’s Progress – for the International Space Station (ISS). The first ATV was launched in 2008, and the fifth and final launched in 2014. However, amid the prospect of Artemis being too expensive, it was decided that the ATV could be adapted into the service module for Orion, saving costs and time. With the evolution of modern technology, the ESM has several advantages compared to the Block II Apollo command and service module (CSM), manufactured by North American Rockwell. The CSM was smaller, with a diameter of just under three metres, compared to the ESM which is four metres. The ESM will also produce more electricity than the CSM due to the use of solar arrays rather than fuel cells, while also weighing significantly less. Further, the ESM can accommodate for missions in deep-space for up to 20 days, compared to the CSM’s 14-day endurance. Artemis I was a huge success for ESA’s ESM. According to manufacturer Airbus, the first flight was a “huge source of information” for the team, and all the mission objectives were achieved. “Initial evaluation of the test data has confirmed that the Orion spacecraft consumed much less propellant and electrical power, while producing much more power than calculated”, Airbus said in a statement in February. “The propulsion subsystem performed as expected delivering the thrust for precise orbital manoeuvres and vehicle attitude control. The good performance of the propulsion system allowed the execution of additional flight test objectives to better characterise the vehicle.” Meanwhile, Airbus said the main engine fired multiple times with a total burn duration of ten minutes as planned. Further, almost two tonnes of propellant were remaining as the mission ended, showing that future missions could be longer. Most impressively, according to Airbus, the solar arrays generated 15% more power than anticipated. However, the reason for this was likely due to the spacecraft consuming less electricity because of the smaller fluctuations in temperature than expected. Trusting in the global four-party team The four Artemis II astronauts take questions from the media at Bremen on 15 September. (Bella Richards/RAeS)The Artemis programme has been heralded as a culmination of a four-party team, which includes NASA, ESA – its 22 member states – Lockheed Martin, and Airbus. The collaboration across several nations is a core distinction from the Apollo era, and this has given the Artemis astronauts even more trust in the system and the people behind keeping them safe. Christina Koch said that meeting people in Europe who will be in the control room during the mission was important for her to trust in the safety of the spacecraft. “We were just in the clean room, and we met the people that are doing every little piece of tape, every connection every mechanical and electrical connector… now when people ask us, are you nervous about this flight, and we say things like we implicitly trust the engineers and the technicians that build this vehicle. Now we've met them, we've seen their work, we've seen how well they do it and how dedicated they are. And that is what matters about this cross-cultural work”, Koch said. The historic launch is fast approaching, and preparations are ramping up. On 11 September, the first of four RS-25 engines were installed onto the core stage of the SLS at NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. This followed the integration of all five major structures of the core stage earlier this Spring, and the remaining three engines are set to be installed soon. Mankind is returning to the Moon, and this time Europe is part of the programme. 22 September, 2023 Space Structures & Materials Training Flight Operations Flight Test News & Features Industry News
